newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Chinese dissident voices concern over HK freedoms.
newsitem.headline: Chinese dissident voices concern over HK freedoms.

text.p: Chinese pro-democracy dissident Chai Ling voiced concern on Monday about the future of freedom in Hong Kong and urged the People's Liberation Army not to repeat the 1989 massacre of protesters in Beijing.
Chai, one of the student leaders who spearheaded the 1989 democracy movement in Beijing's Tiananmen Square, was in Hong Kong for a short visit, just weeks before it reverts to China.

"I am very concerned about how much freedom the people in Hong Kong will be allowed to have after July 1," Chai told a news conference, when asked to comment on moves by Hong Kong's post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa to curb civil liberties.

Tung unveiled his plan to limit protest rights and ban foreign funding of political groups last month. The curbs would take effect on July 1, after Britain hands its 156-year-old colony back to China as a quasi-autonomous capitalist region.
Tung last week softened his package, although the basic principles in the restrictions remain unchanged and are fiercely opposed by Hong Kong's democracy camp.

"That provides a vehicle for the government to control the liberties and freedom of any average citizen and that's really alarming to me," Chai said. Hong Kong people would have to defend their freedom and liberty inch by inch, she said.
Chai also urged PLA garrison soldiers, who will be stationed in Hong Kong to avoid a Tiananmen-like bloodbath there.
Tens of thousands of students and Beijing residents flooded the square in 1989 to urge the government to speed up economic reform and democratisation and weed out corruption.
The army crushed the protest with a heavy loss of life.

"My words to the PLA soldiers who today entered Hong Kong, is to be really respectful to Hong Kong people's basic rights and liberties and freedom. Don't repeat the tragedy that happened eight years ago in Beijing," Chai said.

Sixty-six PLA troops arrived in Hong Kong on Monday, hard on the heels of a first group of 40 soldiers who arrived last month. Another 90 are expected on May 30. The three groups are the advance guard of a garrison that will take over defence duties from Britain immediately after the handover.
Vivid local memories of the crackdown on students on June 4, 1989, in Beijing has made the PLA's entry into Hong Kong a sensitive issue.
Chai said she was now optimistic about China's future because the current economic system of propping up unprofitable state-owned enterprises could not persist.
"Privatisation has to happen, and once that happens, and the issue of ownership and intellectual property rights has to be clarified, human rights will have to be defined again," she said.

A heated power struggle was currently taking place within the Communist Party, she said, following the death of patriarch Deng Xiaoping in February, and a clearer idea of the country's direction would emerge by the end of the year.
Chai said she was on a private visit to the territory to visit friends and was not looking for funding.
The 28-year-old, self-exiled dissident has been studying for a master's degree at Harvard University in the United States and said she hoped ultimately to return to China to work.
Chai will not be in Hong Kong for Tiananmen Square's eighth anniversary memorial. She was only allowed a one-week visa.
She said she did not know why the visa period was just one week.
"It's really unfortunate, I will not be able to attend any June 4 anniversary here in Hong Kong but I've made a commitment to attend the June 4 anniversary in New York," she said.
Chai dismissed a Hong Kong media report which said that she had not stayed with her students to the end, on the night of June 3, 1989, when the PLA moved in.

She said she was among the last students to leave Tiananmen, together with her co-students, when it became clear the PLA had the upper hand. Reporters at the scene in 1989 have corroborated her story.
Chai fled to the West following the crackdown.
